one_liner: Browser MD5 library: RustCrypto md-5 in WebAssembly plus a Web Worker pool, claimed 8-16x faster than spark-md5.
what_it_does: fast-md5-web hashes Files or Uint8Arrays with MD5 off the main thread: Md5CalculatorPool spreads files across a pool of module Web Workers (calculateMd5 with timeout, progress callback and priority; calculateMd5Batch; cancelTask; getPoolStatus), and Md5Calculator exposes the wasm hasher directly (calculate_md5_async plus start/update/finalize incremental sessions). Inputs larger than chunkSize are read in chunks and fed to an incremental hasher, through a SharedArrayBuffer slot when the page is cross-origin isolated, else by transferring ArrayBuffers. It is not a drop-in for spark-md5: the API is promise-based and File-oriented, ESM-only, and returns hex strings of length 32 or 16.
how_it_is_fast: The MD5 compression function is the RustCrypto md-5 0.10.6 crate compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen (release profile opt-level "s", a 59 KB .wasm in the npm package), so the 32-bit add/rotate rounds run as wasm i32 ops instead of JavaScript number arithmetic. Most of the headline speedup comes from parallelism: the pool runs one file per worker, sized by default to navigator.hardwareConcurrency, and a SharedArrayBuffer allocator avoids structured-clone copies when cross-origin isolation is on. MD5 is sequential within one input, so a single large file is hashed by one worker and gains nothing from the pool beyond keeping the UI thread free.
when_to_use: Browser apps that checksum many user-selected files before upload (deduplication, resumable or instant uploads to object storage that wants an MD5) and can spread them over several cores.
When hashing must stay off the UI thread and you want a ready-made pool with per-file timeouts, progress callbacks, priorities and cancellation rather than writing your own worker plumbing.
Sites that already serve Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, so the SharedArrayBuffer path is available (but see the large-file race in gotchas).
Interop with existing MD5-based APIs where the checksum format is fixed; it is a checksum, not a security primitive.
when_not_to_use: Anything security-related (signatures, password hashing, integrity against an adversary): MD5 is not collision resistant.
Hashing one file or a few small buffers: the pool brings no speedup there and the 8x single-thread claim has no published measurement; hash-wasm publishes a reproducible MD5 throughput table.
Large files (above chunkSize) with SharedArrayBuffer enabled until the slot-overwrite race described in gotchas is fixed; disable shared memory or cross-check results.

Node.js servers: node:crypto is native and faster; this package's pool calls new Worker(..., {type: 'module'}) and navigator.hardwareConcurrency, has no worker_threads code despite the README, and WasmInit() by default fetches the .wasm from a URL relative to import.meta.url.
CommonJS projects or toolchains that cannot resolve the worker and wasm files next to dist/ (issue #8 was a Vite import-resolution failure).

integration.dependencies: uuid 11.1.0 at runtime; ships dist/index.js, dist/md5-worker.js and wasm/pkg (wasm-pack --target web output), which the bundler must serve at their relative URLs
integration.min_toolchain: ES2020 ESM consumers; ES module Worker support in the browser; building from source needs Rust, wasm-pack and pnpm (Node >= 18 per engines)
integration.platforms: Browsers (README lists Chrome 68+, Firefox 79+, Safari 15.2+ for SharedArrayBuffer, with HTTPS and COOP/COEP headers); Deno via npm: specifier per README; Node.js only for the direct Md5Calculator with manually supplied wasm bytes
integration.thread_safety: Each worker owns one Md5Calculator; incremental sessions are keyed by task id in a thread_local map inside the wasm module; the pool object is meant to be driven from one thread; not otherwise documented

gotchas: Large-file race (code reading, not reproduced): in SharedArrayBuffer mode processLargeFile writes every chunk into the same single slot, posts calculate_chunk, and moves on after only a microtask yield, with no acknowledgement from the worker; the worker copies the slot when it dequeues the message, so whenever file reads outpace hashing (or the worker is still in WasmInit) a later chunk overwrites an unread one and the MD5 is silently wrong. The same design is in npm 1.1.2 and repo HEAD, and the only large-file e2e test hashes a 300 MB file filled with the single byte 17, where every chunk is identical, so it cannot detect the race.

The published 1.1.2 worker handles messages with an async onmessage and no queue, so chunks of a stream started on a fresh worker can run before WasmInit finishes and fail with 'Stream state not found'; the serial-queue fix exists only in unpublished HEAD (March 2026), which also adds a postinstall that runs pnpm install in the example folder and is not in the package's files list.

Harness flaws behind the 16-17x: the example app times a pool of navigator.hardwareConcurrency workers against spark-md5 running single-threaded on the main thread, always runs spark-md5 first (cold reads) and reports one run on 174 undisclosed files with no hardware or browser; it also configures memorySize 6400 MiB while the comment says 64MB.

md5Length 16 returns the first 16 hex characters (64 bits; the README calls it a '128-bit half'), not the middle 16 that substr(8, 16)-style '16-bit MD5' tools return; small-file SharedArrayBuffer allocations are released only on error or timeout, so the shared region fills and later files silently fall back to copying; calculate_md5_async 'yields' with an already resolved promise, which does not let the browser render, so calling it on the main thread still blocks.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against hash-wasm, which publishes a reproducible single-thread MD5 table (850.31 MB/s vs spark-md5 171.73 MB/s on 1 MB) and covers many algorithms, pick fast-md5-web only when you want its ready-made multi-file worker pool with progress, priority and timeouts and will verify its output; for one file, Node.js or audited numbers, hash-wasm (run in your own worker if needed) is the safer choice.
verified_claims_summary: The only data is one screenshot from the repo's Vue example app: 174 user-selected files, all hashes matching, spark-md5 on the main thread with 2 MB FileReader chunks 109,271.50 ms vs the fast-md5-web pool 6,329.50 ms (17.3x, derived from page data), with hardware, browser, core count and file sizes unstated; the README's 8x single-thread figure and the SharedArrayBuffer 151 vs 200 ms example have no published measurement.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-03-15, MIT, 98 stars) but npm latest is still 1.1.2 from 2025-11-27, so HEAD's worker-queue fix is unpublished; evidence is a single first-party screenshot dominated by parallelism, and the shared-memory large-file path has an unguarded slot-overwrite race that its fixed-byte test file cannot catch.
